usage: 되다 ('work out'), not 하다, is the natural verb: 의사소통이 잘 돼요 frames communication as something that succeeds, not something you do.
Common in workplace and relationship contexts; 문제가 있다 attaches to the abstract process, not to a person.
원활하다 ('smooth, fluid') is the set adjective; the noun form 원활한 의사소통 is near-fixed in business writing.
능력 ('ability') forms a common compound, especially in job ads and self-introductions (자기소개서).
examples: 우리는 손짓으로 간단한 의사소통을 했어요.
We did simple communication with hand gestures.
Graded-simple: 손짓으로 ('with gestures') shows 의사소통 need not be verbal — it is exchange of intent.
부서 간의 원활한 의사소통이 무엇보다 중요해요.
Smooth communication between departments is more important than anything.
Everyday-work register: 부서 간 = 'between departments'; 무엇보다 = 'more than anything'.
오해가 쌓이지 않으려면 솔직한 의사소통이 필요해요.
So misunderstandings don't pile up, honest communication is needed.
Real-situation: 오해가 쌓이다 ('misunderstandings pile up') is the exact collocation; 필요하다 takes 의사소통 as subject with 이/가.
nuance: 의사소통 is the formal, slightly academic word for 'communication' as the exchange of thoughts and intentions, built from the hanja 意思疏通 (意思 'intention/meaning' + 疏通 'flowing through, unblocking'), so the literal image is 'making intentions flow through'. The nearest near-synonym is 대화, but the dividing line is clear: 대화 is one concrete spoken conversation, while 의사소통 is the whole skill or process of getting understanding across — which can even happen by gesture or writing. In casual speech Koreans clip it to 소통, especially when praising someone open and approachable (저 사람은 소통이 잘 돼). The big English-speaker pitfall is the verb: do not say 의사소통을 하다 by reflex the way you'd say 'do communication'; the idiomatic frame is 의사소통이 잘 되다/안 되다 (communication works / doesn't), treating it as something that succeeds with 이/가, not an action you perform.

mistakes: Using 대화 ('conversation') when you mean 'communication' as a skill or process — 대화 is one specific talk, 의사소통 is the broader ability to convey intent, so 의사소통 능력 (not 대화 능력) is what a job ad asks for.
Saying 의사소통을 하다 too literally on the model of English 'do/have communication'; Koreans far more often say 의사소통이 잘 돼요 / 안 돼요 to describe whether it actually works.
Treating 소통 and 의사소통 as different words — 소통 is just the casual clip of the same concept, so don't over-formalize friendly speech with the full four-syllable form.

usage: 하다 is the standard verb, and 토론하다 also works as one word; the topic attaches with ~에 대해.
벌어지다 ('unfold, break out') is natural for a lively, spontaneous debate, more dynamic than 하다.
찬반 ('for and against', 贊反) is the set modifier for a structured two-sided debate, common in school.
주제 ('topic', 主題) forms a common compound for the set issue under discussion.
examples: 우리 반은 오늘 짧은 토론을 했어요.
Our class did a short debate today.
Graded-simple: 토론을 하다 is the core frame; 짧은 토론 shows it can be brief and classroom-scale.
이 주제는 찬반 토론을 하기에 아주 좋아요.
This topic is great for a pro-and-con debate.
Everyday: 찬반 토론 = the set phrase; ~하기에 좋다 = 'good for ~ing' attaches the activity to a judgment.
토론에서는 상대방의 의견도 끝까지 들어야 해요.
In a debate you have to listen to the other side's opinion to the end.
Real-situation: teaches register — 토론 demands 상대방 ('the other party', a polite formal word) and 끝까지 ('to the very end').
nuance: 토론 (討論, 討 'examine/discuss' + 論 'argue, treatise') is an organized, rule-based discussion where people exchange and defend opinions on a set topic — classroom debates, panel discussions, formal meetings. Place it on a spectrum between two near-synonyms: it is more structured and goal-oriented than 대화 (relaxed everyday conversation), yet calmer and more cooperative than 논쟁 (a heated dispute where sides clash). The dividing line from 논쟁 is intent: a good 토론 stays respectful and aims to weigh views, even when people disagree, whereas 논쟁 carries friction. Natural collocations are 토론을 벌이다/하다, 찬반 토론, 토론 주제. The English-speaker pitfall is over-using 'debate/discuss' for any back-and-forth: a casual chat with friends is 대화 or 이야기, never 토론 — reserve 토론 for a deliberate, topic-driven exchange.

mistakes: Confusing 토론 (a structured, civil debate) with 논쟁 (a heated argument); 토론 aims to exchange and examine views, 논쟁 implies open conflict and emotion.

Pairing the topic with the wrong particle — say 환경 문제에 대해 토론하다 ('debate about ~'), not 환경 문제를 토론하다 in careful speech.

usage: to engage in / wage an argument
벌이다 ('start, wage') is the idiomatic verb for an active, ongoing dispute between sides.
일어나다 ('arise') is natural when a dispute breaks out on its own from some trigger.
뜨겁다 ('hot') is the set temperature metaphor; 뜨거운 논쟁 = a fierce, passionate dispute.
to be open to dispute / debatable
여지 ('room', 餘地) in a fixed phrase: literally 'there is room for argument', i.e. it's arguable.
examples: 그 말 한마디가 작은 논쟁을 일으켰어요.
That one remark caused a small argument.
Graded-simple: 논쟁을 일으키다 ('cause an argument'); 말 한마디 = 'a single remark'.
인터넷에서 그 문제를 두고 뜨거운 논쟁이 벌어졌어요.
A heated argument broke out online over that issue.
Everyday-online: ~을/를 두고 = 'over (an issue)'; 벌어지다 = 'break out'; 뜨거운 논쟁 is the set phrase.
이건 논쟁의 여지가 없는 명백한 사실이에요.
This is an obvious fact that leaves no room for dispute.
Real-situation: the negative idiom 논쟁의 여지가 없다 ('no room for argument'); 명백하다 ('obvious') reinforces it.
nuance: 논쟁 (論爭, 論 'argue/discourse' + 爭 'contend, fight for') is a heated argument or public controversy in which sides clash, often emotionally or over high-stakes issues — note the 爭 'contend' character that 토론 lacks, which is exactly where the friction lives. The nearest near-synonym is 토론, and the dividing line is conflict: 토론 is an orderly, cooperative exchange of views, while 논쟁 is adversarial and charged, with people pushing to win. It is also broader and more public/intellectual than a personal quarrel (싸움 or 다툼). Habitual collocations: 논쟁을 벌이다, 논쟁이 일어나다, 뜨거운 논쟁, 논쟁의 여지가 있다/없다, and the adjective 논쟁적이다 ('controversial'). The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 논쟁 for a personal fight between friends — that is 싸움/다툼; 논쟁 belongs to issues and ideas, typically in public or written contexts, not bickering.

Saying 논쟁을 하다 when describing an unfolding clash — the more vivid, idiomatic choice is 논쟁을 벌이다 (wage) or 논쟁이 벌어지다 (break out).

usage: 하다 form; 설득하다 is the common one-word verb, and it takes the PERSON as object: 친구를 설득하다.
성공하다 ('succeed') and 실패하다 ('fail') pair naturally, framing persuasion as an attempt with an outcome.
설득 + 력 (力 'power'); 설득력이 있다/없다 = to be / not be persuasive, an extremely common judgment.
당하다 makes the passive: you ended up convinced by someone, sometimes against initial resistance.
examples: 동생을 설득해서 같이 갔어요.
I persuaded my younger sibling and we went together.
Graded-simple: note 동생을 (person as direct object); ~해서 chains 'persuaded, so (then)'.
그 사람의 주장은 설득력이 있어요.
That person's argument is persuasive.
Everyday: 설득력이 있다 = 'to have persuasive power', a key intermediate phrase you'll hear constantly.
아무리 설득해도 그는 끝내 마음을 바꾸지 않았어요.
No matter how much I tried to persuade him, in the end he didn't change his mind.
Real-situation: 아무리 ~해도 = 'no matter how much ~'; 마음을 바꾸다 = 'change one's mind'.
nuance: 설득 (說得, 說 'speak/explain' + 得 'obtain, gain') is the act of persuading someone to accept your view or do something — literally 'gaining them by speaking', i.e. winning agreement through reasoning rather than force. The crucial near-synonym contrast is with 강요 (強要 'coercion'): 설득 wins willing agreement, while 강요 imposes against the person's will, so they are ethically opposite. The derived noun 설득력 ('persuasiveness') is everyday vocabulary — Koreans judge arguments by whether 설득력이 있다 or 없다. The sharpest English-speaker pitfall is the particle on the object: 설득하다 takes the PERSON directly with 을/를 (친구를 설득했어요), unlike the English frame 'persuade someone OF something', so learners wrongly produce 친구에게 설득했어요. Use 설득에 성공하다/실패하다 to talk about the result.

Marking the object with 에게 — say 친구를 설득했어요 (person as direct object), never 친구에게 설득했어요, because 설득하다 governs the person with 을/를.
Translating English 'I have no power to persuade' loosely — the Korean noun is 설득력 (없다), so say 설득력이 없어요, not a word-by-word rendering.

usage: 하다 form; 협상하다 also works as a single verb; the counterpart attaches with ~와/과.
결렬되다 ('break down', 決裂) is the standard news verb for talks that collapse.
negotiations are concluded / reach a deal
타결되다 ('be settled', 妥結) is the fixed counterpart for a successful outcome.
협상 테이블에 앉다 = 'sit at the negotiating table', a common idiom for entering talks.
examples: 가격을 두고 잠깐 협상을 했어요.
We negotiated briefly over the price.
Graded-simple: ~을/를 두고 협상하다 = 'negotiate over ~'; 잠깐 keeps it small-scale.
임금 협상이 결국 결렬되었어요.
The wage negotiations ultimately broke down.
Everyday-news: 임금 협상 = 'wage negotiations'; 결렬되다 = 'fall through', the set failure verb.
양측은 며칠간의 협상 끝에 합의에 이르렀어요.
After several days of negotiation, both sides reached an agreement.
Real-situation: 협상 끝에 = 'after negotiation'; 합의에 이르다 = 'reach an agreement', formal register.
nuance: 협상 (協商, 協 'cooperate/jointly' + 商 'discuss, deliberate, trade') is formal negotiation between parties with differing interests — business deals, labor talks, diplomacy — literally 'jointly deliberating' toward a mutually acceptable compromise. The everyday near-synonym to contrast is 흥정: 흥정 is informal haggling over a single price at a market or with a vendor, whereas 협상 is structured, institutional, and higher-stakes. News reports fix its outcome with the paired verbs 타결되다 (reach a deal, 妥結) versus 결렬되다 (break down, 決裂) — memorize them as opposites. Other set collocations: 협상 테이블에 앉다, 협상을 벌이다. The English-speaker pitfall is using 협상 for casual bargaining ('I negotiated the price down at the market'), which should be 흥정했어요; also keep 타결 and 결렬 straight, since swapping them inverts whether the deal succeeded or collapsed.

Marking the other party with 에게 — the counterpart in negotiation attaches with ~와/과 (회사와 협상하다), not 에게.

usage: 하다 is the standard verb; 연설하다 also works; the audience attaches with ~앞에서 ('before').
연설 + 문 (文 'writing'); the written script an address is read from or prepared as.
취임 ('taking office', 就任) + 연설; a common fixed compound, also 축사 for congratulatory addresses.
감동적이다 ('moving', 感動的) is the natural modifier for a memorable, emotionally powerful address.
examples: 반장이 친구들 앞에서 짧은 연설을 했어요.
The class president gave a short speech in front of the others.
Graded-simple: 앞에서 = 'in front of'; shows 연설 needs an audience, even a small one.
그의 졸업식 연설은 정말 감동적이었어요.
His graduation speech was truly moving.
Everyday: 졸업식 연설 = 'graduation speech'; 감동적이다 = the set adjective for a stirring address.
대통령의 취임 연설이 전국에 생중계되었어요.
The president's inauguration speech was broadcast live nationwide.
Real-situation: 취임 연설 = fixed compound; 생중계되다 = 'be broadcast live', formal news register.
nuance: 연설 (演說, 演 'perform/expound' + 說 'speak') is a formal spoken address delivered to an audience — by a politician, a graduate, a public figure — almost always prepared in advance, the literal sense being 'to expound by speaking'. Two near-synonyms mark its borders: it differs from 발표 (a presentation of information, results, or a project, where the point is content/data) and from 강의 (a lecture meant to teach). The dividing line is purpose: 연설 aims to address and often inspire a gathered audience, not to instruct or report. Habitual collocations: 연설을 하다, 취임 연설, 감동적인 연설, 연설문. The English-speaker pitfall is stretching 연설 to any 'speech': a few informal words or a toast at a small gathering is 인사말 ('a few words of greeting') or 건배사 (a toast), and a project briefing is 발표 — reserve 연설 for the prepared, formal public address.

Two near-synonyms mark its borders: it differs from 발표 (a presentation of information, results, or a project, where the point is content/data) and from 강의 (a lecture meant to teach). The dividing line is purpose.
演說: 演 'perform/expound' + 說 'speak' — the literal sense being 'to expound by speaking'.

Don't stretch 연설 to any 'speech': a few informal words or a toast at a small gathering is 인사말 ('a few words of greeting') or 건배사 (a toast), and a project briefing is 발표 — reserve 연설 for the prepared, formal public address.

mistakes: Confusing 연설 (a prepared public address) with 발표 (a presentation of a project, results, or information) — the goals differ: inspire/address versus inform/report.
Using 연설 for an informal toast or a few words at a small gathering — for that say 인사말 ('a few words') or 건배사 (a toast).
Saying 연설을 말하다 by translating 'give a speech' loosely — the verb is 연설을 하다 (or 연설하다); 말하다 doesn't collocate here.

usage: 듣다 ('listen') is the idiomatic verb — you 'hear' a lecture or course; never 받다 or 배우다.
From the teacher's side; 강의하다 also works as one verb (교수님이 강의하다).
온라인 강의 became extremely common; the older slang clip is 인강 (인터넷 강의).
강의 + 실 (室 'room'); the physical room where a university lecture is held.
examples: 이번 학기에 역사 강의를 들어요.
I'm taking a history course this semester.
Graded-simple: 강의를 듣다 = the idiomatic 'take a course'; note 듣다, literally 'listen'.
그 교수님의 강의는 항상 인기가 많아요.
That professor's lectures are always very popular.
Everyday: 인기가 많다 = 'be popular'; 교수님 carries the honorific ~님 for a professor.
요즘은 집에서 온라인 강의를 들을 수 있어요.
These days you can take online lectures from home.
Real-situation: 온라인 강의 = set compound; ~을 수 있다 = 'can', highlighting the convenience.
nuance: 강의 (講義, 講 'expound/teach' + 義 'meaning, principle') means a lecture or an academic course, especially at university level, where a teacher expounds material to students — the hanja literally 'expounding the principles'. The key near-synonym is 수업: 수업 is the general word for a class at ANY level (elementary, middle school, a tutoring session), while 강의 leans academic and university, with a content-delivery, one-direction feel. The signature collocation is the verb 강의를 듣다 ('listen to a lecture') for attending or taking a course — this is the heart of the English-speaker pitfall, because learners reach for 받다 ('receive') or 배우다 ('learn') on the model of 'take/receive a course'; both are wrong, the only natural verb is 듣다. Other collocations: 강의를 하다 (teach side), 온라인 강의, 강의실.

usage: 하다 form; used for BOTH the interviewer and the interviewee side, so context decides who.
to agree to / give an interview
응하다 ('comply, respond to', 應) is the formal verb for accepting a request to be interviewed.
인터뷰 + 기사 (記事 'article'); a written press piece based on an interview.
방송 ('broadcast') marks the medium, distinguishing it from a print or job interview.
examples: 그 배우가 방송에서 인터뷰를 했어요.
That actor gave an interview on the broadcast.
Graded-simple: 인터뷰를 하다 works for the interviewee here; 방송에서 = 'on air'.
기자가 시민들과 거리에서 인터뷰를 진행했어요.
A reporter conducted interviews with citizens in the street.
Everyday-press: 인터뷰를 진행하다 = 'conduct an interview'; ~와 = 'with (the interviewee)'.
내일 회사 면접이 있어서 너무 떨려요.
I have a job interview at the company tomorrow, so I'm really nervous.
Real-situation: deliberately uses 면접 (not 인터뷰) — a hiring interview is standardly 면접 in Korea.
nuance: 인터뷰 is a loanword (from English 'interview') covering media and research interviews — a reporter questioning someone, or the Q&A of gathering a story or opinion. The essential near-synonym contrast for learners is with 면접 (面接, 'face-meeting'): a JOB/admissions interview is standardly 면접, while 인터뷰 leans toward press, broadcast, celebrity, or research questioning. You will hear 면접 인터뷰 too, but for hiring, default to 면접. Natural collocations: 인터뷰를 하다, 인터뷰에 응하다, 인터뷰를 진행하다, 인터뷰 기사. The two big English-speaker pitfalls: first, defaulting to 인터뷰 for a job interview (say 면접); second, the verb for 'be interviewed' — English makes it passive ('I was interviewed'), but Korean says 인터뷰를 하다 (the interviewee also 한다) or the formal 인터뷰에 응하다, never 인터뷰를 받다.

usage: to appear on a broadcast / be on TV
나오다 ('come out') = appear on air from the viewer's side; 방송에 나가다 ('go out') = air, from the producer's side.
생 ('raw, live') + 방송; a real-time broadcast, contrasted with 녹화 방송 (pre-recorded).
방송 + 국 (局 'bureau/station'); the company or organization that broadcasts, e.g. KBS, MBC.
to make it onto a broadcast
타다 ('ride') idiomatically = to get aired and gain attention, often used when a place suddenly goes viral on TV.
examples: 그 가수가 오늘 방송에 나와요.
That singer is on a broadcast today.
Graded-simple: 방송에 나오다 = 'appear on TV', the most basic frame; ~에 = the air/program.
이 프로그램은 매주 금요일 저녁에 생방송으로 진행돼요.
This program airs live every Friday evening.
Everyday: 생방송으로 = 'live (as a live broadcast)'; ~으로 진행되다 = 'be run/aired as'.
그 식당은 방송을 탄 뒤로 손님이 줄을 서요.
Ever since that restaurant got on TV, customers line up.
Real-situation: the idiom 방송을 타다 ('ride the broadcast' = get aired and go viral); 줄을 서다 = 'line up'.
nuance: 방송 (放送, 放 'release/send out' + 送 'send') covers both the act of broadcasting and a specific TV or radio program — the hanja image is 'sending out (a signal)'. There isn't one tidy synonym to contrast; instead, learn its internal map: 생방송 (live, 生) versus 녹화 방송 (pre-recorded, 錄畫), and the directional pair 방송에 나오다 (appear, viewer's view) versus 방송에 나가다 (go on air, producer's view). The vivid idiom 방송을 타다 ('ride the broadcast') means something got aired and drew attention. The English-speaker pitfall is conflating 방송 with neighboring words: 채널 is the 'channel', 프로그램 is a specific 'program/show', and 방송 is the airing/broadcast itself — so for a named show, 프로그램 is clearer than 방송. Also note 방송 frequently appears as a verb 방송하다 ('to broadcast').

mistakes: Confusing 방송 (a broadcast / the airing) with 채널 ('channel') or 프로그램 ('a specific show') — 방송 is the broadcasting/airing itself, not the slot or the title.
Mixing up 방송에 나오다 (appear on air, said by a viewer) and 방송에 나가다 (go on air, said from the production side) — the direction of 나오다 vs 나가다 flips the perspective.
Forgetting the contrast 생방송 (live) vs 녹화 방송 (pre-recorded) and calling a taped show 생방송 — 생 specifically marks real-time airing.

usage: 나빠지다 / 악화되다 ('worsen', 惡化) describe collective sentiment souring; 여론 is the subject with 이/가.
여론 + 조사 (調査 'survey'); written as one compound, the standard term for a public poll.
형성하다 ('form', 形成) is the formal verb, often with media as the agent that shapes opinion.
여론 paired with 관심 ('interest') for what the public collectively cares about.
examples: 그 사건 이후로 여론이 나빠졌어요.
After that incident, public opinion turned negative.
Graded-simple: 여론이 나빠지다 = 'opinion sours'; 이후로 = 'after, ever since'.
최근 여론조사에서 그 정책에 대한 반대가 높게 나왔어요.
In a recent poll, opposition to that policy came out high.
Everyday-news: 여론조사 = the compound 'opinion poll'; 높게 나오다 = 'come out high'.
언론은 여론을 형성하는 데 큰 역할을 해요.
The press plays a big role in shaping public opinion.
Real-situation: 여론을 형성하다 = 'shape opinion'; ~는 데 역할을 하다 = 'play a role in ~ing', formal civic register.
nuance: 여론 (輿論, 輿 'public/the multitude, the carriage of the people' + 論 'discourse, opinion') is public opinion — the collective views and mood of society on an issue, especially as measured by polls or reflected in media. The sharp near-synonym contrast is with 의견 ('opinion', 意見): 의견 is one individual's view (제 의견은...), while 여론 is always the aggregate sentiment of the public — you cannot have a personal 여론. Because it is a collective abstract noun, it takes characteristic verbs: 여론이 나빠지다, 여론이 들끓다 ('boil over'), 여론이 형성되다. Set collocations: 여론조사, 여론을 형성하다, 여론의 관심. The English-speaker pitfall is using 여론 for a single person's opinion ('in my opinion'), which must be 제 의견에는 / 제 생각에는, never 여론; also write 여론조사 as one compound, not loosely as 여론 조사.

Pairing 여론 with 말하다 ('여론을 말하다') — opinion of the public is shaped/measured: 여론이 형성되다, 여론조사를 하다, not 'spoken'.

english: the press; the media (as an institution)
usage: to be reported in the press
보도되다 ('be reported', 報道) is the standard passive paired with 언론; the press is the medium with ~에.
자유 ('freedom', 自由) in a fixed civic phrase about the press's rights and independence.
언론 + 사 (社 'company'); a newspaper or broadcaster as a business entity.
언론 + 보도 (報道 'report'); how the media collectively covered an event.
examples: 그 사건이 언론에 크게 보도됐어요.
That incident was reported widely in the press.
Graded-simple: 언론에 보도되다 = the core passive; 크게 = 'in a big way, widely'.
언론의 자유는 민주주의의 중요한 기둥이에요.
Freedom of the press is an important pillar of democracy.
Everyday-civic: 언론의 자유 = the fixed phrase; 기둥 = 'pillar', a common metaphor for a foundation.
여러 언론사가 같은 사건을 다르게 보도했어요.
Several news organizations reported the same event differently.
Real-situation: 언론사 = 'news organization (as a company)'; 보도하다 = 'report (news)', active form.
nuance: 언론 (言論, 言 'speech/words' + 論 'discourse') refers to the press or news media as a social institution — newspapers, broadcasters, and journalists collectively, together with their public role of informing society; the hanja literally evokes 'public speech/discourse'. Contrast three near terms learners blur: 언론 is the institution, 뉴스 is the news content you watch/read, and 신문 is one specific newspaper. There is also 미디어 (loanword 'media'), but in formal civic discussion of the press's role and rights, 언론 is the standard, weightier term (언론의 자유, never 미디어의 자유 in serious usage). Habitual collocations: 언론에 보도되다, 언론의 자유, 언론사, 언론 보도. The English-speaker pitfall is swapping 언론 with 뉴스 or 미디어 — 'I saw it on the press' should map to 뉴스/언론 보도, and the institution that holds 'freedom of the press' is specifically 언론.

usage: 글을 올리다 ('put up a post') is the standard verb; 글 ('a written post') is the thing you upload, with ~에 for the board.
자유 ('free', 自由) + 게시판; the open, anything-goes section of a community site.
a notice appears on the board
뜨다 ('come up, pop up') is natural for a post or notice showing up on screen.
질문 ('question', 質問) + 게시판; the section where users post questions for others to answer.
examples: 게시판에 사진을 한 장 올렸어요.
I posted one photo on the board.
Graded-simple: 올리다 = 'upload/put up'; 한 장 uses the counter 장 for flat things like photos.
궁금한 점이 있으면 자유게시판에 글을 남기세요.
If you have questions, leave a post on the open board.
Everyday: 글을 남기다 = 'leave a post' (alt. of 올리다); 궁금한 점 = 'something you're curious about'.
그 글이 게시판에서 큰 화제가 되었어요.
That post became a big topic of discussion on the board.
Real-situation: 화제가 되다 = 'become a hot topic'; ~에서 marks the board as the location of buzz.
nuance: 게시판 (揭示板, 揭示 'to post up, display' + 板 'board/plank') is a bulletin board — both the physical kind (a notice board on a wall) and the online kind (a forum or message board on a website); the hanja literally means 'display board'. Online, the key system of collocations is: you 글을 올리다 ('upload a post') or 글을 남기다 ('leave a post') on a 게시판, and others respond underneath with 댓글 ('comments', 답글 for a direct reply). The near concept to keep distinct is 댓글 — the 게시판 is the structured space where original posts (글) live, while 댓글 are the replies attached to a post; don't confuse the container with the comments. It also contrasts with live 채팅 (chat), which is real-time. The English-speaker pitfall is saying 게시판에 쓰다 ('write on the board') alone for posting — the idiomatic phrasing needs the object 글: 게시판에 글을 올리다/남기다.

Using 글을 내리다 carelessly for 'delete' — 글을 내리다 means take a post down/unpublish it; to erase it you 글을 삭제하다.

usage: 쓰다 is the standard verb from the journalist's side; 기자가 기사를 쓰다 ('a reporter writes an article').
an article comes out / is published
나다 ('come out') is idiomatic for an article appearing in print or online.
신문 ('newspaper', 新聞) + 기사; the most common compound for a print article.
검색하다 ('search', 檢索) for finding articles online, e.g. by keyword or date.
examples: 오늘 신문에서 기사를 하나 읽었어요.
I read one article in today's newspaper.
Graded-simple: 신문에서 = 'in the newspaper'; 하나 counts the article casually.
그 사건에 대한 기사가 모든 신문에 났어요.
An article about that incident came out in every newspaper.
Everyday: ~에 대한 기사 = 'an article about ~'; 기사가 나다 = 'an article comes out', the set verb.
요즘은 종이 신문보다 온라인 기사를 더 많이 봐요.
These days I read online articles more than paper newspapers.
Real-situation: 온라인 기사 = 'online article'; ~보다 더 많이 = 'more than ~', a comparison frame.
nuance: 기사 (記事, 記 'record/write down' + 事 'matter, event') means a news article or report — a single written piece of journalism in a newspaper, magazine, or online; the hanja literally means 'a written record of an event'. Distinguish it carefully from neighbors: 언론 is the press as an institution, 보도 (報道) is the ACT of reporting, and 기사 is the concrete written unit of content that results. A crucial English-speaker pitfall is the homonym trap: 기사 is also a completely separate word meaning 'driver' (司機/운전기사) — and historically 'knight' (騎士) — so 택시 기사 is 'taxi driver', not 'taxi article'; only context tells which 기사 is meant. Natural collocations: 기사를 쓰다, 기사가 나다, 신문 기사, 기사를 검색하다. Don't reach for 기사 when you mean the abstract media institution — that is 언론.

Saying 기사를 만들다 ('make an article') by translating loosely — a reporter 기사를 쓰다 (writes it); 만들다 doesn't collocate with a news article.
